description: We are a passionate and enthusiastic team of students interested in science, technology, innovation and problem-solving. Our goal is to collaborate, explore real-world challenges and develop creative solutions using scientific knowledge and technology. We welcome individuals from different backgrounds with diverse skills, fresh ideas and a shared passion for innovation and space exploration.
summary: This project identifies Earth-based environments that serve as partial analogues for lunar and Martian exploration. It examines locations such as the Atacama Desert, Antarctica, Haughton Crater, Iceland, Hawaii, Lonar Crater, Rio Tinto and Svalbard. Each site is evaluated for specific similarities in geology, climate, landforms and terrain to support planetary research. The study highlights their potential for testing exploration technologies, studying extreme environments and preparing for future Moon and Mars missions, while acknowledging the limitations of Earth-based comparisons.
details: Project Overview SELENOVAQ – Earth Analog Explorer is a project that identifies and compares locations on Earth that have environmental and geological similarities to potential permanent Moon base locations and Mars exploration sites. The main aim is to understand how Earth environments can help scientists prepare for future human space exploration. 2. Selected Earth Analog Locations The project studies several locations around the world: - Atacama Desert, Chile: An extremely dry environment with terrain useful for Mars analog research. - McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica: A cold and dry environment for studying extreme conditions. - Haughton Crater, Canada: An impact crater that provides opportunities for planetary geology research. - Askja, Iceland: A volcanic landscape useful for studying planetary surface processes. - Mauna Loa, Hawaii: Volcanic terrain that helps researchers understand geological features. - Lava Beds, California, USA: An area with volcanic formations and lava features. - Lonar Crater, India: An impact crater with important geological research value. - Rio Tinto, Spain: An iron-rich environment relevant to astrobiology studies. - Svalbard, Norway: An Arctic environment useful for studying extreme conditions. 3. How the Project Works The project uses comparative research to examine the terrain, geology, climate, and surface characteristics of these locations. It presents their similarities and differences with possible lunar and Martian environments. A conceptual map and comparison matrix help users understand the selected locations. 4. Benefits and Intended Impact SELENOVAQ demonstrates how Earth-based research can support future Moon and Mars missions. It can help students and researchers understand planetary geology, extreme environments, habitat challenges, and the importance of selecting suitable locations for scientific testing and astronaut preparation. 5. Tools and Resources The project uses NASA planetary science resources, publicly available Earth observation information, research articles, comparative analysis, and a conceptual location-screening approach. 6. Creativity and Innovation The project connects Earth science with space exploration by presenting real-world locations as research analogs for future lunar and Martian missions. 7. Limitations The selected locations are preliminary research candidates, not confirmed sites for permanent bases. Further scientific investigation, field studies, and engineering assessments would be required before selecting actual mission locations.
